text: Mint New Coinage
The books will not balance and the armies are owed, my lord. A new issue struck at a lighter weight would cover the shortfall within the month, though the merchants will know what we have done.
Patronage of the Arts
We have the schools and the temples, my lord, but nothing to make a learned man wish to teach in them. Endow the academies and the wealthy will follow the scholars here.
Host a Tournament
There are men in your court with nothing to prove and nobody to prove it against, my lord. Announce the lists and let them fight for your name before a crowd.
Reward Heroism
This general came back from the field with the enemy's standards, my lord. Grant the honours publicly, and with them the instruction of the finest masters your gold can summon.
Court Examination
Your halls are thin of talent, my lord. Announce an examination and the provinces will send us their best, already schooled and ready for a post.
Reassess the Rolls
This one has been overlooked for years, my lord, and the rolls do him no justice. Reassess his record and give him the rank his service has already earned.
Purge the Corrupt Officials
The tax rolls and the treasury no longer agree, my lord, and the difference is sitting in a great many private houses. Purge the offices, though those who remain will not thank you.
Tax Amnesty
The people are near the end of what they will bear, my lord. Forgive this season's taxes and they will remember it far longer than the revenue would have lasted.
Open the Granaries
There is hunger in the provinces and grain in your stores, my lord. Open the granaries now and the gratitude will outlast the winter.
Grand Review of Troops
Your armies have not stood together under your eye in years, my lord. Call a grand review; the men march the better for having been counted.
Summon a Physician
This general suffers from an affliction he will not speak of, my lord. Send for a physician of real skill before it costs you the man entirely.
Grant Land to the Gentry
The local families have been loyal and have had little for it, my lord. Grant them land and their tenants will work it harder than any levy of ours could manage.
Expand the Black Office
Our people abroad are underpaid and working out of borrowed rooms, my lord, which is how such men come to talk. Give the office its own budget and they will keep their footing.
Unmask the Informers
There are ears in this court that are not ours, my lord. Let us find them, and make the next ones far more expensive to place.
Convene the Scholars
There is a question the ministry has circled for years, my lord, and the men who could settle it are scattered across three provinces. Summon them and it will be decided this season.
Retrench the Court
The treasury cannot carry this court much longer, my lord. Cut the stipends to the bone; your ministers will be furious and your armies will still be paid.
Quarter the Army on the Land
Feeding the army from the granaries is bleeding us, my lord. Quarter them on the villages instead and the upkeep falls, though the villages will not enjoy it.
Levy the Corvee
There is work to be done and no coin to pay for it, my lord. Call up the corvee; the roads and walls will rise cheaply, and the people will grumble about it for a season.
Contract the Free Companies
The captains who ride for us sell their swords to whoever asks first, my lord, and others have been asking. Negotiate the contracts now, as a body, and the price falls sharply.
Provision the Marches
The marches will kill more of your men this season than the enemy will, my lord. Lay in the depots now and the columns will come back whole.
Post Riders on the Roads
Word from the far commanderies reaches us weeks late, my lord. Man the relay stations properly and your orders will arrive while they still mean something.
Send the Envoys
We are a rumour in courts we have never visited, my lord. Send envoys with gifts to every hall that will receive them, and become a name they recognise rather than one they distrust.
Open the Silk Routes
The passes are open and nobody is minding them, my lord. Clear the roads, garrison the caravanserai and post an honest toll, and the caravans will come to us.
Resettle the Displaced
The roads are full of people with nowhere to go, my lord, and your cities have room for them. Settle them, feed them through the season, and they will be yours.
Open the Coffers
Your ministers have served through lean years without complaint, my lord. Open the coffers and pay them what the work was worth; loyalty bought now is bought cheaply.
Spread Sedition
Their provinces are quieter than they deserve, my lord. A little coin in the right hands and their magistrates will have troubles enough of their own to attend to.
Blight Their Harvest
Their granaries are their strength, my lord. Men can be paid to be careless with a torch at harvest, and nothing will ever be proven against us.
Buy Out Their Merchants
Their wealth runs through a handful of trading houses, my lord. Buy those houses out from under them and the loss will be felt for years.
Denounce Them Abroad
Their name still carries weight in courts that should know better, my lord. Let us see it ruined, politely and in writing, in every hall that matters.
Suborn Their Commander
One of their generals believes he is owed more than he has been given, my lord. He is not wrong, and he is not expensive.
Bribe Their Quartermasters
An army is only as good as the men who count its carts, my lord. Those men are poorly paid, and they will count very badly indeed for very little.
Vassal Tribute
Our tributaries pay what was agreed and not a coin more, my lord, while their granaries fill. Revise the terms upward; every court will note how you treat those who submit to you.
Promote Industry
Our forges and workshops are an afterthought beside our neighbours', my lord. Second the surveyors and remit the levies, and the next foundry will rise faster and cheaper than the last.
Promote Commerce
For all the roads that pass through us we have built little to profit by them, my lord. Put the state's carpenters and the state's money behind the markets and the wharves for a season.
Promote the Land
Too many households are crowded onto too little worked ground, my lord. Fund the waterworks, the granaries and the field roads at our expense rather than the districts' own.
Promote Learning
We have grain and we have soldiers, my lord, and almost nothing to make an educated man stay. Endow the schools and the temples, and make it cheap to raise more of them.
Seek a Weapon
There are blades in this country worth more than the men who carry them, my lord, and most do not know it. Send buyers to the smithies and the estate sales and see what returns.
Seek Armour
Good harness outlives the man it was forged for, my lord, and a great deal of it has lain in chests since the rebellion. Put out word that we are buying, and pay without haggling.
Seek a Mount
The horse a general rides is the first thing an army sees of him, my lord. Send agents to the northern herds and the breeders' fairs with orders not to return empty-handed.
Seek a Follower
Every court of consequence has its physicians, its diviners and its quiet men of business, my lord. Ours is thin in all three. Let it be known that we are hiring, and generously.
Seek a Curiosity
Seals, manuals and jade mark a court as one worth attending, my lord. Send collectors out with a purse and no very precise instructions as to how they spend it.
Divide the Spoils
This one did not come to you for a salary, my lord. Let him open the strongroom before his own men and hand it out by the fistful; it is not how a ministry does things, and that is the point.
Levy the Hill Country
There are men in the high valleys who have never paid a tax and never will, my lord, but who will march for someone who speaks their dialect. We happen to have such a man.
Compile the Commentaries
Give this one a room, a stipend and some quiet, my lord, and he will produce a commentary that outlives all of us. We cannot spare him years, but we can spare him the room.
Permit Plain Speech
He has asked leave to say what he actually thinks in open council, my lord. Grant it; the accounts will be honest for a season and a good many officials will discover urgent business elsewhere.
Let His Name Precede Him
Send this one ahead of the column with a modest escort and orders to be seen, my lord. Half the villages between here and the border have argued about him over dinner.
The Champion's Example
Put him in front of the recruits for a season rather than in front of the enemy, my lord. They will drill until they drop for a man they have heard songs about.
The Agricultural Garrisons
The land between the ruins is good and nobody is left to work it, my lord, while your soldiers eat through a granary a season. Settle them on it: soldiers in spring, farmers in summer.
Benevolence Proclaimed
The refugees on the road are choosing which lord to walk toward, my lord, and they have been choosing you. Say plainly what you intend for them, and see that it is true when they arrive.
The Tiger's Pace
He does not wait for the baggage, my lord, and the men have stopped expecting him to. Formalise it: light columns, forward depots, and orders written for where the army will be.
Four Generations, Three Excellencies
There is not a court in the empire where your family name needs explaining, my lord. Spend it. Send the letters under your seal and let four generations of Excellencies argue for you.
Strip the Capital
The palaces are full of things that cannot be eaten and the treasury is full of nothing, my lord. Melt what can be melted, sell what can be sold, and let the histories say what they like.
The Longzhong Plan
He has drawn the whole empire on a single sheet, my lord, and marked which powers will fight each other without our help. Act on it and we shall discover whether he is right.
Wait for the Wind
He advises doing nothing, my lord, at length and with unnerving precision about when the nothing should end. Fund the watchers and let the men in a hurry exhaust themselves.
The Scholar in Armour
He reads ground the way other men read a ledger, my lord, and the columns he plans arrive with their boots intact. Give him the marching orders and the supply tables both.
White Clothes Crossing the River
Merchants going upriver in white, poling quietly, with the armour in the bottom of the boat, my lord. Nobody challenges a merchant until the beacon towers are already ours.
No Man Rides Ahead of Him
He will not hold the centre and he will not wait for the order, my lord. Write the plan around a man who is always half a day further forward than anyone intended him to be.
The Little Conqueror
He takes a commandery in the time it takes the ministry to appoint a clerk for it, my lord. Supply the column properly and send the administrators after him, several weeks behind.
Hold What My Brother Took
You will not conquer the south a second time, my lord; it is already yours. Settle the garrisons, pay the tribute, and be remembered as the man it stayed with.
The Court Governs Itself
He signs what is put before him and asks after the gardens, my lord. A chancellery that governs unsupervised is a cheap one, and what the ministers take on the side is the price of it.
The Nine Ranks
Grade every official one to nine and appoint strictly by the grade, my lord. It is fairer than what we do now, and the great families will have it gamed within a decade.
The White Horse Fellows
Every man on a white horse and every horse chosen for the road, my lord. The steppe has learned what the colour means; keep the remounts coming and it will keep meaning it.
The Rites Observed
He proposes we do the thing properly, my lord: the full ceremonies, the schools endowed, the descendants of Confucius seated where they belong. It will cost us a season's revenue.
The Peace of Jing
While the north burns the scholars keep arriving here with their libraries on carts, my lord. Do nothing to disturb it; garrison the passes, feed the newcomers, and let Jing stay quiet.
Close the Roads to Yi
The passes into Yi can be held by very few men against very many, my lord. Close them, build inward, and let the rest of the empire wonder what we are doing behind them.
The Liang Horsemen
Liang breeds more horses than it can feed and more riders than it can employ, my lord. Take both. They will eat everything we have and nothing on this frontier can catch them.
Xu Province Endures
He is old and tired, my lord, and he has kept Xu fed through two rebellions without raising the grain tax. Fund whatever he is doing and stop asking him to explain it to the ministry.
The Seal Is Ours
The seal is in your keeping, my lord, and a seal in one's keeping is very nearly a mandate. Say so loudly and in writing; every court will take offence and every court will be talking.
The Bandit Queen's Word
Her word in the hills is worth more than your seal on paper, my lord, and she has never once broken it. Let her give it on your behalf; the accounting will be creative and the peace real.
The Black Mountain
A hundred thousand men live in those valleys, my lord, and not one has been paid in coin. They want salt, grain and to be left alone in winter, which is an army at a fraction of the cost.
The White Tiger's Toll
Every barge on the lower river already pays him something, my lord. Formalise it into a toll with a posted rate; the merchants will complain about the rate and be relieved about the receipt.
The Old Alliance of Liang
He has sworn brotherhood with half the chieftains west of the pass and outlived most of them, my lord. The oaths still bind their sons; send him to collect while the sons remember why.
The Governor of Bing
Bing is poor, exposed and full of people who would rather be governed by us than by the steppe, my lord. That is a low bar and a real advantage. Build while they still feel that way.
King of Hexi
He has already taken the title, minted the coin and appointed the ministers, my lord. Grant it retroactively and in fifty years the histories will not be able to tell the difference.
The Northern Peace
He would rather trade with the Wuhuan than fight them, my lord, and for twenty years it has worked. Fund the frontier markets, keep the tribute flowing, and send the war party elsewhere.
The Henei Levy
Henei has been raising and losing armies since the alliance, my lord, and has grown very good at the raising. Use the machinery; the men are cheap, willing and available again next spring.
The Quiet Marches
He has kept a road open through four years of other men's wars by taking no side loudly, my lord. Use the road: depots at every stage and no banners on the carts.
The White Wave Bargain
His men were rebels last year and will be again the moment the grain stops, my lord. Until then they are the cheapest infantry in the empire and they ask no questions.
The Prince's Purse
A prince of the Han with a full treasury and no army worth the name is a very specific kind of asset, my lord. Take the money and the legitimacy both, and keep his household in its accustomed style.
The Captains' Contract
The free companies will ride for him personally and haggle with everyone else, my lord. Have him do the negotiating; the rate drops the moment they see whose seal is on the contract.
The Scholar's Circle
Half the promising young men in the province write to him, my lord, and a fair number of the dangerous ones. Give the correspondence a roof and a stipend and see what comes of it.
The Hall of Repose
Exhausted men make bad decisions slowly and then defend them, my lord. Open the hall and order the rota as an instruction rather than a favour; nobody will thank you and everybody will sleep.
The Calligrapher's Hand
An order in his hand is obeyed faster than the same order in anyone else's, my lord. That is either a point about authority or a comment on our clerks; either way, have him write the important ones.
The Duke's Oath
He returned the gifts, left the seal on the table and rode back to a man who had nothing to offer him, my lord. Every soldier knows the story; let it be known he serves you and say nothing further.
Drink and Discipline
He can turn a mob into a battle line in a fortnight, my lord, by methods the ministry would prefer not to record. Give him the recruits and do not visit the camp.
The Escort of the Heir
He came out of a lost field carrying a child and said nothing of it afterwards, my lord. Put him where the people who matter to you are, and stop worrying about them.
The Western Riders
The Qiang follow him and not us, my lord, which is worth remembering. They will ride the length of the frontier while our infantry is still forming up.
The River Is Ours
He knows which channels take a loaded hull in low water and which villages will sell grain to a fleet, my lord. Give him the river and the campaign stops depending on the roads at all.
The Southern Tribes
His people cross ground that kills our columns and think nothing of it, my lord. Bring them in on their own terms, which are simpler than ours and mostly involve being left alone afterwards.
Open the Armoury at Ye
The captains ride for you already, my lord, in whatever harness they could afford. Open the armoury and let them draw from the state stores at the state's price.
Borrowed Banners
The captains who answer to us answer to Yuan Shao first, my lord, and everyone involved knows it. Pay the difference, fly his colours where it helps, and take the men.
Blood the New Captains
The companies are willing and green, my lord, a combination that gets men killed in the first engagement. Give them a season of real work under officers who have survived one.
Debased Coinage
The new cash rings thin, and everyone from the salt merchants to the market watch knows it.
Patronage of the Arts
Scholars, artisans and their wealthy admirers have made your court their own.
The Grand Tournament
For a season the commanderies talk of nothing but the lists, the wagers and the winner.
Tournament Injury
The fall was worse than it looked, and it will be some months before the arm answers properly.
Renown of the Tournament
Word of the victory is travelling further than any proclamation could.
Laurels of the Lists
The crowd knows the name now, and so does the champion. Winning again simply renews this.
The Crowd's Favour
The lists were a good day out and the grain was free. Winning again simply renews this.
Beaten in the Lists
He was unhorsed in front of half the commandery, and he will hear about it for a while.
Honoured for Valour
He has been decorated before the whole court and set to study under the finest masters available.
The Examination Halls
The halls are open, the examiners are seated, and the candidates are queued into the street.
Advanced by Merit
Overlooked for years, he has been raised in an afternoon to the grade his record always warranted.
The Inspectors' Purge
The ledgers are honest again, and the clerks who kept them are considerably less comfortable.
Tax Amnesty
This season's levy has been remitted in full, and the commanderies have noticed.
The Granaries Opened
State grain is moving into the district markets under your banner.
Grand Review
Every standard has been inspected and every complaint heard, and the men are the better for it.
Under the Physician's Care
He is in competent hands, and sleeping properly for the first time in a long while.
Gentry Estates
The great houses have been settled on the land and are working it with a will.
The Black Office
The office has quiet rooms and a real budget, and is keeping its people abroad rather better.
Watchers on the Watchers
Foreign agents are finding this court a markedly less comfortable place to work.
The Assembled Scholars
The scholars are shut in with the archives until the matter is settled, and the court is paying for all of them.
Retrenchment
Stipends have been cut and attendants dismissed; the treasury breathes and the court sulks.
Quartered on the Land
The regiments are dispersed into the villages, fed and housed by the districts they sit in.
The Corvee
Labour service has been called up, so the works rise quickly and the fields go untended.
The Free Companies
Contracts have been signed with the border captains in advance, and at a considerable discount.
Provisioned Marches
Salt, grain and felt have been laid in along the roads before the campaigning season opens.
The Post Roads
The relay stations are manned at proper intervals, with fresh horses waiting at every one.
Envoys Abroad
Gifts and reassurances have been delivered to every hall that would receive them.
The Silk Routes
The passes are cleared and the caravanserai garrisoned, with an honest toll posted for every merchant to read.
Resettlement
The roads are emptying as the displaced take up land, seed and a year's exemption.
The Coffers Opened
Stipends have been raised and arrears settled; it is expensive, and the court has noticed.
Sedition Abroad
Someone has been putting coin and grievance into the wrong hands out in the commanderies.
The Blighted Harvest
The fields burnt in the season when nothing can be replanted, and the granaries will be light.
The Merchants Bought
The great trading houses have found a better arrangement elsewhere and taken the routes with them.
Denounced Abroad
An account of their worst decisions is circulating in every court that matters.
A Commander Courted
Someone has been agreeing with him, at length, about everything he is owed.
The Carts Miscounted
The men who count the fodder have been paid to count it badly.
Revised Tribute
The tributaries are paying rather more than they agreed to, and everyone knows it.
Industry Promoted
Surveyors have been seconded and levies remitted, so workshops, forges and mines rise faster and cheaper.
Commerce Promoted
State carpenters and state money are behind the markets, the wharves and the trade roads.
The Land Promoted
Waterworks, granaries and field roads are being raised at the treasury's expense rather than the district's.
Learning Promoted
Schools, temples and tea houses are endowed, and cheaper to raise than they have ever been.
Buyers at the Smithies
Agents have been sent to every forge and estate sale with instructions to buy.
Buyers for Armour
Word is out that the court is buying harness, and paying without haggling.
Agents at the Horse Fairs
Buyers have been dispatched to the northern herds and the breeders' fairs.
The Court Is Hiring
Physicians, diviners and men of business have been invited to present themselves.
Collectors Dispatched
Collectors have been sent out with a purse and no very precise instructions.
The Spoils Divided
He handed it out by the fistful before the men who earned it, and they will not forget who allowed it.
The Hill Country Levy
The hill men are cheap and willing, and behaving exactly as badly as expected.
The Commentaries
He has a room, a stipend and as much quiet as a war allows.
Plain Speech Permitted
The accounts are honest for a season, and a good many officials have been posted elsewhere.
His Name Precedes Him
He is being seen in the squares and argued about at every dinner table between here and the border.
The Champion's Example
The recruits are drilling past exhaustion for a man they have heard songs about.
The Agricultural Garrisons
The garrisons soldier in spring and farm in summer, and the grain never has to be carted anywhere.
Benevolence Proclaimed
The promise was made plainly and kept when the refugees arrived, and word of that travels.
The Tiger's Pace
The columns are light and the depots forward, and orders are written for where the army will be.
Four Generations, Three Excellencies
The letters go under a seal that needs no explanation, carried by officials who expect to be paid like it.
The Capital Stripped
The capital has been melted, sold and carted out, and the histories will say what they always would.
The Longzhong Plan
The whole empire is drawn on one sheet, with the wars we do not have to fight marked out.
Waiting for the Wind
The watchers are funded, the court is patient, and the men in a hurry are tiring themselves.
The Scholar in Armour
The marching orders and supply tables are written by the same hand, and the column arrives intact.
White Clothes on the River
Merchants are poling quietly upriver with the armour in the bottom of the boat.
No Man Rides Ahead of Him
The plan is written around him rather than at him; the court is furious and the enemy is late.
The Little Conqueror
The columns are moving faster than the clerks who are supposed to follow them.
Hold What Was Taken
The garrisons are settled and the tribute paid by a house that means to be here in thirty years.
The Court Governs Itself
The ministers govern unsupervised, delighted, and are helping themselves at a steady rate.
The Nine Ranks
Every official is graded and appointed by the grade, and the great families are reading it carefully.
The White Horse Fellows
The remounts are kept up, and the steppe has learned to read the colour at a distance.
The Rites Observed
The ceremonies are observed in full and the schools endowed, and a season's revenue is quietly gone.
The Peace of Jing
The passes are garrisoned and the refugees fed, and the army has grown very comfortable indeed.
The Roads Closed
We are building inward behind held passes, and the plain is left to guess at it.
The Liang Horsemen
There are more riders than we can feed, moving faster than anything that might object.
Xu Endures
The granaries are run by a tired old man who has never yet had to raise the grain tax.
The Seal Displayed
The claim has been made loudly and in writing; everyone has taken offence and everyone is talking.
The Queen's Word
The accounting is creative and the peace in the hills actually holds.
The Black Mountain
The army is paid in salt and grain, and the magistrates are left to cope.
The White Tiger's Toll
There is a posted rate and a receipt, which is more than the merchants had before.
The Old Alliance
The old oaths are being collected from the sons of the men who swore them.
The Governor of Bing
We are building fast in a province that has decided it prefers us to the alternative.
King of Hexi
The title was taken and then granted retroactively, and nobody will be the wiser in fifty years.
The Northern Peace
The frontier markets are funded, the tribute flows, and the war party has been sent elsewhere.
The Henei Levy
The province has become extremely practised at replacing its own army.
The Quiet Marches
There are depots at every stage and no banners on the carts, and the road is still open.
The White Wave Bargain
They are the cheapest infantry in the empire, for exactly as long as the grain lasts.
The Prince's Purse
The treasury is full, and a princely household expects to be kept in the style it is used to.
The Captains' Contract
The rate drops the moment the captains see whose seal is on the contract.
The Scholar's Circle
The province's promising young men are under one roof and on a stipend.
The Hall of Repose
The rota was nobody's idea and the court has finally slept.
The Calligrapher's Hand
The important orders are written in the one hand nobody argues with.
The Duke's Oath
A story every soldier already knows is now attached to your banner.
Drink and Discipline
He has turned a mob into a battle line in a fortnight, and nobody visits the camp.
The Escort of the Heir
The people who matter are placed behind the one man nobody has to worry about.
The Western Riders
The riders follow him rather than us, and cover ground nobody else can.
The River Is Ours
The channels, depots and grain villages are his, and the campaign no longer needs the roads.
The Southern Tribes
They cross the killing ground without noticing it, on terms of their own.
The Armoury at Ye
The captains have been re-horsed and re-armed from the state stores, at the state's price.
Borrowed Banners
Another man's captains are flying another man's colours and doing our work.
The New Captains Blooded
The new companies are getting a season of real work under officers who have survived one.

Champion of the Realm

Your man took the meeting outright, and the shouting went on long after the crowd should have gone home. He will be spoken of in commanderies that have never heard your name — which is, of course, rather the point.
Carried From the Lists
It was not a clean fall, and he did not get up on his own. The physicians expect a recovery, in time. The tournament, however, will finish without him.
One Man Could Be Spared
Only one of your officers was free to ride, so there was nothing to decide. He has the colours and the ground is marked; the rest is up to him.
The Lists Stand Empty
Your champion is dead, and there is no one at court with either the standing or the appetite to take his place mid-season. The heralds have been sent to call the thing off.
Unrest in the Commanderies
Reports arrive of coin changing hands in market squares and old grievances suddenly finding their voice. Somebody is paying for this, and it is not one of your magistrates.
The Fields Are Burning
Riders came through the farmland at night with torches and salt, in the one season when nothing can be replanted. The granary counts for next year will make grim reading.
The Trading Houses Withdraw
The great merchant families have quietly accepted a better offer elsewhere, and the caravan routes have gone with them. Your customs officers are standing at empty gates.
Denounced in Every Court
A carefully assembled account of your worst decisions is being read aloud in halls you have never visited. Enough of it is true to make the rest stick.
A Commander's Grievance
One of your generals has been receiving a great deal of sympathetic correspondence about how badly he has been used. He appears to have found it persuasive.
The Carts Do Not Add Up
The fodder counts are wrong, and have been for some time. Your quartermasters are either incompetent or have been paid to appear so.
